questions.question: In which month and year did Mahatma Gandhi return to India from South Africa?
questions.explanation: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi returned to India on 9 January 1915 (a landmark date commemorated annually in modern India as Pravasi Bharatiya Divas) at the age of 45, after spending over two decades in South Africa. In South Africa, he had developed and perfected the novel method of mass mobilization and moral resistance known as 'Satyagraha' (holding firmly to truth through non-violent passive resistance) to fight racial segregation and discriminatory laws against the Indian immigrant community. Upon his arrival in India, on the advice of his political mentor Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Gandhi spent his first year travelling extensively across the country by third-class railway carriages to understand the ground reality of Indian masses. (NCERT Class 10 History Chapter 2, Section 1).

questions.question: Mahatma Gandhi organized his first successful Satyagraha in India in 1917 at Champaran (Bihar) to support peasants against:
options: Low wages in cotton textile mills
questions.explanation: After returning from South Africa in January 1915, Mahatma Gandhi successfully organized his very first Satyagraha campaign on Indian soil in 1917 at Champaran, Bihar. He was persuaded by local peasant Raj Kumar Shukla to visit Champaran and investigate the plight of sharecroppers forced under the oppressive British 'Tinkathia' system to plant indigo on 3/20th of their fertile land. Gandhi's non-violent moral resistance inspired the peasants, leading to the appointment of an official inquiry committee and the refund of illegally extorted dues. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 1.1).

questions.question: On which historic date did the infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place in Amritsar?
questions.explanation: The Jallianwala Bagh massacre occurred on the fateful afternoon of 13 April 1919 (the traditional Punjabi harvest festival of Baisakhi) in Amritsar. A large, peaceful crowd had gathered in the enclosed ground of Jallianwala Bagh—some to celebrate the Baisakhi mela and others to protest peacefully against the arrest of nationalist leaders Dr. Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal under the repressive Rowlatt Act. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer entered the area with British-Indian troops, blocked the sole narrow exit with armored vehicles, and ordered his riflemen to open continuous fire without issuing any dispersal warning, firing 1,650 rounds until ammunition was exhausted, brutally killing hundreds of men, women, and children. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 1.2).

questions.question: Who renounced his British Knighthood in deep anguish and protest following the Jallianwala Bagh massacre?
questions.explanation: On 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi Day), Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer ordered British troops to open fire without warning on a large, peaceful gathering trapped in the walled compound of Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing hundreds. In deep moral anguish and protest against this barbarous massacre, Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British Knighthood (awarded in 1915). In his poignant letter to the Viceroy Lord Chelmsford, Tagore stated that the time had come when badges of honour made our shame glaring in the context of humiliated fellow countrymen. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 1.2).

questions.question: At which Congress session in December 1920 was the Non-Cooperation programme finally ratified and adopted?
questions.explanation: During the autumn of 1920, intense internal debates took place within the Indian National Congress regarding the proposed boycott of legislative councils. However, at the historic Congress session held at Nagpur in December 1920, an amicable compromise was forged among faction leaders, and the Non-Cooperation movement resolution was formally ratified and adopted. The Nagpur Congress also amended its constitution to establish a 15-member Congress Working Committee (CWC) and re-organized Provincial Congress Committees along linguistic lines. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 1.3).

questions.question: Who led the peasant movement in Awadh against oppressive talukdars and landlords during the Non-Cooperation Movement?
questions.explanation: In the rural countryside of Awadh (present-day eastern Uttar Pradesh), the agrarian peasant movement was led by Baba Ramchandra—a charismatic sanyasi who had earlier served as an indentured sugar plantation labourer in Fiji. The Awadh peasants faced crushing oppression from aristocratic talukdars and wealthy landlords, who demanded exorbitant land rents (lagaan), illegal cesses, and compulsory unpaid forced labour ('begar'). The peasant movement demanded a reduction of land revenue, abolition of begar, and a social boycott of oppressive landlords organized through local 'nai-dhobi bandhs'. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 2.1).

questions.question: In October 1920, the Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up and headed by:
options: Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra, and a few others
Mahatma Gandhi and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Subhas Chandra Bose and Bhagat Singh
questions.explanation: In June 1920, Jawaharlal Nehru began touring the villages of Awadh, holding discussions with rural peasants and assessing their deep agrarian grievances. By October 1920, the historic 'Oudh Kisan Sabha' was formally instituted, jointly headed by Jawaharlal Nehru, Baba Ramchandra, and local peasant organizers. Within one month of its founding, the organization's popularity surged, and over 300 grassroots village branches were established across the region. When the Non-Cooperation Movement began the following year, the Congress worked to integrate the Awadh peasant struggle into the wider anti-colonial nationalist campaign. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 2.1).

questions.question: Who led the militant guerrilla movement of tribal peasants in the Gudem Hills of Andhra Pradesh in the early 1920s?
questions.explanation: In the dense forest tracts of the Gudem Hills in Andhra Pradesh, a militant guerrilla movement erupted in the early 1920s among tribal villagers, led by Alluri Sitaram Raju. The colonial British forest laws had closed large forest reserves, preventing tribal communities from grazing their cattle, collecting fuelwood, or shifting cultivation, and coerced them into forced labour (begar) for road construction. Sitaram Raju, whom the tribals believed possessed miraculous healing powers and could survive bullet wounds, claimed inspiration from Gandhi's Non-Cooperation movement and persuaded people to wear khadi and give up alcohol, while asserting that India could be liberated only through force, not non-violence. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 2.2).

questions.question: Which leaders formed the Swaraj Party within the Congress in 1923 to argue for a return to council politics?
options: Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and M.R. Jayakar
questions.explanation: Following the sudden withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement by Mahatma Gandhi after the violent Chauri Chaura incident in February 1922, sharp tactical divisions arose within the Congress. Chittaranjan Das (C.R. Das) and Motilal Nehru advocated entering the newly reformed Legislative Councils set up under the Government of India Act 1919 to expose colonial legislative flaws and oppose British policies from within. In January 1923, they founded the 'Congress-Khilafat Swaraj Party' (commonly called the Swaraj Party) within the Congress framework, while younger leaders like Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose pressed for direct radical mass agitation and full independence. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 3.1).

questions.question: Why was the Simon Commission boycotted by all political parties upon its arrival in India in 1928?
options: It recommended dividing India into twenty provinces
It was headed by General Dyer
It did not have a single Indian member
It demanded immediate introduction of martial law
questions.explanation: In November 1927, the British Conservative government constituted an Indian Statutory Commission under Sir John Simon to review the working of the Government of India Act 1919 and recommend constitutional reforms. The commission sparked nationwide outrage because it did not include a single Indian representative; all seven appointed commissioners were white British parliamentarians. When the commission landed in Bombay in February 1928, it was greeted with black flags and universal protest chants of 'Simon Go Back' by the Congress, Muslim League, and Hindu Mahasabha. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 3.1).

questions.question: Under whose presidency did the Lahore Congress Session in December 1929 formalize the historic demand of 'Purna Swaraj' (complete independence)?
questions.explanation: In December 1929, the historic annual session of the Indian National Congress was held on the banks of the river Ravi in Lahore under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru. The Lahore Congress formally adopted the historic resolution demanding 'Purna Swaraj' (complete and unconditional independence from British colonial rule), superseding all earlier demands for dominion status within the British Empire. The session also declared that 26 January 1930 would be celebrated across the country as 'Independence Day', when citizens would take a solemn pledge to struggle for total independence, a historic date later chosen in 1950 for the enforcement of the Constitution of India. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 3.1).

questions.question: From where did Mahatma Gandhi begin his historic 240-mile Salt March on 12 March 1930?
questions.explanation: On 12 March 1930, Mahatma Gandhi launched the Civil Disobedience Movement with his historic Salt March (Salt Satyagraha). Accompanied by 78 handpicked, trusted ashram volunteers, Gandhi set out on foot from his Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad toward the coastal village of Dandi on the Gujarat seacoast, traversing a distance of over 240 miles (385 km) over 24 days. On 6 April 1930, after reaching the seashore at Dandi, Gandhi ritually picked up a lump of natural salt from the beach, boiling seawater to manufacture salt and ceremonially breaking the British colonial salt monopoly law that imposed an unfair tax on a basic dietary necessity consumed equally by the rich and the poor. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 3.2).

questions.question: Who was devoutly referred to as 'Frontier Gandhi' and organized the Khudai Khidmatgars in the North-West Frontier Province?
questions.explanation: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan (1890–1988), passionately revered across the subcontinent as 'Frontier Gandhi' (Badshah Khan), was a devout Pashtun follower of Mahatma Gandhi. In 1929, he founded the 'Khudai Khidmatgars' (Servants of God), a dedicated non-violent volunteer army whose members wore red shirts (the 'Red Shirts'). When British authorities arrested Ghaffar Khan in Peshawar in April 1930 during the Civil Disobedience Movement, angry demonstrations erupted, and platoon soldiers of the Garhwal Rifles famously refused to open fire on the peaceful crowds. (NCERT History Chapter 2, Section 3.2).
